page_contents_html:
DRAFT for local agreement — not for clinical use. Aligned to the national CfSD Genetic Haemochromatosis pathway (September 2026). Items marked [TO AGREE] need a local decision before publication.

Background

Most raised ferritin is not iron overload. Only around 10% of patients with a raised serum ferritin have iron overload; the usual causes are alcohol, metabolic syndrome / MASLD, inflammation, infection and malignancy. Ferritin is only acted on as possible iron overload when the transferrin saturation (Tsat) is also raised (>45%).

Genetic haemochromatosis (GH) in this pathway means iron overload in a patient who is homozygous for p.C282Y in the HFE gene. Diagnosis requires both the genotype and biochemical iron overload — penetrance is variable (serious iron overload in around 30–35% of male and 5–10% of female C282Y homozygotes). H63D homozygotes and carriers of a single mutation are not at risk of clinically significant iron overload. C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity is not disease-causing on its own.

Most patients are managed in primary care. Refer only C282Y homozygotes with biochemical iron overload, and patients with unexplained ferritin persistently ≥1000 ng/mL despite addressing lifestyle factors. Early treatment of GH prevents cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma and allows normal life expectancy.

accordion_sections.heading: Assessment
accordion_sections.html:
When to check ferritin and iron studies

  • Chronic unexplained fatigue or weakness
  • Early-onset arthralgia or atypical arthropathy (typically 2nd/3rd MCP joints and ankles)
  • Abnormal LFTs or liver disease of unknown cause — ferritin and Tsat are part of the non-invasive liver screen and iLFT protocol
  • Less common: early-onset erectile dysfunction, early menopause or loss of libido; early-onset arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy; unexplained increasing skin pigmentation
  • Family screening: adult (≥18 years) siblings and children of a C282Y homozygote with GH (see Primary care management)

Step 1 — serum ferritin, when the patient is well. Do not test during acute illness or for 6 weeks afterwards. Use the local laboratory reference range.

No further iron tests needed if ferritin is:

  • <200 ng/mL in pre-menopausal women
  • <300 ng/mL in men and post-menopausal women
  • or below the upper reference range (URR) of the local laboratory

Step 2 — early-morning fasting transferrin saturation (Tsat) if ferritin is above these levels. Ferritin and Tsat can be requested together or in sequence.

At the same time, look for the common causes of a raised ferritin: FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, HbA1c, lipids, alcohol history (units/week), BMI.

Step 3 — HFE genotype only when there is biochemical iron overload:

Request HFE genotype if Tsat >45% AND

  • ferritin >200 ng/mL in pre-menopausal women, or
  • ferritin >300 ng/mL in men and post-menopausal women, or
  • ferritin above the local laboratory URR

Do not request HFE testing when Tsat is ≤45%, or when ferritin is normal.

How to request: EDTA sample to biochemistry marked “Haemochromatosis genotype”. For family screening, give the affected relative’s name, DOB, health board and the family mutation if known. No genetic counselling or referral to Clinical Genetics is needed.

Interpreting the genotype

  • C282Y/C282Y (homozygote) — GH if biochemical iron overload is present. See Who to refer / Primary care management.
  • C282Y/H63D (compound heterozygote) — not disease-causing on its own; mild iron overload usually reflects alcohol or metabolic syndrome. Manage in primary care.
  • H63D/H63D, single C282Y or H63D (carrier), or no mutation — not at risk of clinically significant iron overload from HFE. Manage the raised ferritin as for any other cause.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
1. Raised ferritin — not GH (Tsat ≤45%, or HFE genotype other than C282Y/C282Y)

  • Take a detailed alcohol history and assess for metabolic syndrome.
  • Investigate abnormal LFTs with a full non-invasive liver screen, and offer BBV testing where there are risk factors.
  • Calculate FIB-4 where there is MASLD or alcohol risk. FIB-4 >1.3 (>2.0 if aged over 65): follow the D&G liver fibrosis pathway. [TO AGREE 8: link to the local liver fibrosis / FibroScan pathway]
  • Give lifestyle advice: alcohol reduction, weight management, smoking cessation.
  • Repeat iron studies after 12–18 months. If ferritin is ≤500 ng/mL and there is no advanced fibrosis, no further follow-up is needed.
  • Ferritin persistently ≥1000 ng/mL despite effective lifestyle change and with no clear explanation: refer (see Who to refer).

Patients with a clear alternative explanation (for example alcohol excess or metabolic syndrome) do not need referral.

2. C282Y/H63D compound heterozygote

  • No biochemical iron overload: reassure and discharge. Give liver health advice. The patient may self-refer to SNBTS to donate blood.
  • Ferritin above URR but <1000 ng/mL: manage as for raised ferritin above (alcohol, metabolic syndrome, FIB-4, lifestyle, repeat at 12–18 months). No referral.
  • Ferritin ≥1000 ng/mL despite effective lifestyle change: refer.

3. C282Y homozygote WITHOUT biochemical iron overload — manage in primary care; do not refer.

  • Offer family screening (below).
  • Advise avoiding iron and vitamin C supplements.
  • Tell them about blood donation: patients who have never been venesected can self-refer to SNBTS (Scotblood).
  • Annual ferritin and Tsat until age 65. Refer if iron overload develops. [TO AGREE 4: practice recall method / Read code for this register]
  • At 65, review whether monitoring is still worthwhile, based on frailty, co-morbidity and likely benefit.

Family screening

  • Offer ferritin, Tsat and HFE genotype to adult (≥18) siblings and children of a C282Y homozygote with GH.
  • Test parents only after an individual decision based on age, sex and ferritin.
  • Relatives are usually asymptomatic. Their GP requests the tests. [TO AGREE 9: local patient leaflet to give to relatives]

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Refer to the D&G Haemochromatosis Service [TO AGREE 1: host specialty (gastroenterology/hepatology or haematology), named clinical lead, and SCI Gateway referral route]

  • C282Y homozygote with biochemical iron overload (Tsat >45% and ferritin above the thresholds in Assessment).
  • C282Y/H63D compound heterozygote with ferritin ≥1000 ng/mL despite effective lifestyle change.

Ferritin ≥1000 ng/mL in a C282Y homozygote means a higher risk of liver fibrosis and needs direct liver stiffness assessment. [TO AGREE 3: referral priority for ferritin ≥1000 — the national pathway does not specify urgent; the current local page says urgent]

Unexplained ferritin persistently ≥1000 ng/mL without a GH genotype, despite effective lifestyle change and with no clear alternative cause

Refer for specialist evaluation (possible MRI liver iron quantification, testing for rare HFE or non-HFE iron overload). [TO AGREE 2: receiving specialty — haematology, or the Haemochromatosis Service]

Refer via the existing liver pathway (not this pathway)

  • Any patient with FIB-4 >1.3 (>2.0 if over 65), cirrhosis, or signs of chronic liver disease — follow the D&G liver pathway, whatever the genotype.

Include in the referral: HFE genotype, ferritin and Tsat (with dates), FBC, LFTs, HbA1c, FIB-4, alcohol intake, BMI, and relevant co-morbidity.

While waiting, patients can be signposted to the British Liver Trust — haemochromatosis.

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
• Raised ferritin with Tsat ≤45% — iron overload unlikely; manage the underlying cause.
  • C282Y homozygotes without biochemical iron overload — annual ferritin and Tsat in primary care until 65.
  • C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes with ferritin <1000 ng/mL — primary care management.
  • H63D homozygotes, carriers of one mutation, and non-carriers — not at risk of HFE iron overload.
  • Raised ferritin with a clear alternative explanation (alcohol excess, metabolic syndrome / MASLD, inflammation) — manage the cause.
  • Ferritin tested during acute illness or within 6 weeks of it — repeat when well.
  • Family members for testing only — the GP requests ferritin, Tsat and HFE genotype.

accordion_sections.heading: Venesection and follow-up
accordion_sections.html:
After referral, every new patient is seen in a nurse-led GH clinic (fibrosis assessment, baseline bloods, contraindication check) and discussed at the GH MDT. The MDT decides whether venesection is likely to help. Frail, elderly or highly co-morbid patients may not benefit. [TO AGREE 1: GH MDT membership (gastroenterology/hepatology, haematology, GH nurse), frequency and format]

Who delivers venesection

The national pathway uses a secondary care, nurse-led service. In D&G, venesection may be done in GP practices under the venesection LES, working to a written specialist plan. This is a local variation from the national pathway, because of the region’s rural geography. [TO AGREE 5: which phases practices deliver — maintenance only, or depletion as well; where depletion happens for practices not in the LES (hospital clinic, CTAC, neighbouring practice); LES funding and uptake]

Specialist plan — issued by the GH service before practice venesection starts

  • Volume (usually 450–500 mL) and frequency (weekly or fortnightly)
  • Target ferritin and date of the next ferritin check
  • Any B12/folate replacement
  • Named contact for results and advice [TO AGREE 6: escalation route — GH nurse phone line / shared inbox; who reviews ferritin results and updates the plan]

At each venesection session

  • Check for temporary contraindications: systolic BP <100 mmHg, intercurrent illness, pregnancy, stroke in the last 6 months, iron-deficiency anaemia, poor venous access. If present, defer and inform the GH service.
  • FBC at every session.
  • Hb <120 g/L — reduce frequency. Hb <110 g/L — pause and inform the GH service.

Permanent contraindications (e.g. active cancer, terminal illness, severe or uncontrolled cardiac disease) are reviewed by the GH MDT.

Depletion phase

  • 450–500 mL weekly or fortnightly, following a personalised plan.
  • Ferritin after every 4–6 sessions until it falls to 200 ng/mL, then every 1–2 sessions.
  • Target ferritin 50–100 ng/mL. A ferritin within the reference range may be accepted by agreement between the patient and the team.
  • Patients in the depletion phase should avoid raw or undercooked shellfish (Vibrio vulnificus risk).

Maintenance phase

  • Usually 2–6 venesections a year; FBC at each session, ferritin every 6 months.
  • Target ferritin within the reference range (<300 ng/mL men and post-menopausal women; <200 ng/mL pre-menopausal women).
  • Cirrhosis: stays in secondary care for venesection (target 50–100 ng/mL) and 6-monthly ultrasound and AFP.
  • Iron-deficiency anaemia or an unexplained fall in venesection need: consider blood loss and investigate as usual.
  • Annual review in the nurse-led GH clinic (face to face, virtual, telephone or patient-initiated). Agree the plan and target ferritin for the year ahead. [TO AGREE 7: service capacity to provide annual review for all patients, including those venesected in practice or donating]
  • At 65, the MDT reviews whether to continue. Patients with no end-organ damage and a life expectancy under 10 years may stop. Anyone continuing is reviewed every 1–2 years.

Blood donation (SNBTS)

  • Stable maintenance-phase patients can be referred by the GH service to SNBTS, using the SNBTS GH referral form. To be eligible they need no end-organ damage, good venous access, no adverse reactions, and no need for IV fluids.
  • Donation is at most every 12 weeks, with Hb 125–165 g/L (women) or 135–180 g/L (men). The usual upper age limit of 65 can be waived at SNBTS discretion.
  • SNBTS does not notify the GH team. Patients must report their donations at annual review.
  • Donation is always optional. Patients who cannot or do not want to donate continue with service or practice venesection.
  • [TO AGREE 10: availability of SNBTS donor sessions in D&G]
